items_missed: No agenda statement and no confirmation ask. 'I can just kind of reset. I can just kinda start from the beginning' tells the customer he is starting over but not what the next fifteen minutes will cover or how long it will take. She had already been through this once with another rep and gotten nothing — a roadmap was worth more to her than to most callers.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up.

Packing services never offered, and the customer raised packing twice. First unprompted: 'we'll have to still pack our stuff up. But like, we are, we haven't really packed.' Then again later, as the explanation for her own confusion over a number: 'that was when I was doing potentially having you all packed for me, never mind.' She said the words 'having you all pack for me' out loud and it was never quoted. That is a revenue miss on a booked job with fifty to sixty boxes still unpacked, and it is also an estimate risk — if she runs out of time and asks the crew to pack on move day, the six-hour estimate is gone.

Storage never probed. The customer mentioned 'we also have like storage bin' and 'we got married. So we have like, things still in those boxes' — it was never established whether anything is coming from an offsite unit.

Clock section is a complete zero on a job that booked. The clock start ('billable time begins when we arrive and open the contract') was never explained, the 2.5-hour minimum was never mentioned, fifteen-minute proration was never mentioned, and there was no sense-check anywhere in the pricing block. A customer is now on the schedule for Sunday with a $1,287 number in her head and no idea how the billing actually works — which is exactly the setup for a move-day dispute, and this is a customer who told him she 'had really bad experience with our last movers.'

'Pricing is super simple' was said, but about booking rather than pricing — 'with us too, we're super simple. If you do want to book at any point we don't require any deposits.' The opener never framed the rate explanation itself.

What's-included list was gestural rather than specific: 'everything is included like we were talking about... we have wrap everything, disassemble reassemble whatever we need to do.' Gas, truck, taxes, insurance, pads, bands and tools were never itemized.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned. He came close — 'the movers they'll give you a call at around eight on the morning of just kind of let you know when they're heading your way' and a good stretch on crew vetting — but the pre-move email with the mover's photo and info never came. On a customer whose stated objection is a bad prior mover experience, putting a face and a name in her inbox days early is the single most reassuring thing Einstein offers, and she got the adjacent version of it instead.
Truck count never stated. Movers yes, trucks no.
No equivalents or plain-language anchor used to make the hours concrete.

Specialty items never worked as a time variable. The Peloton was named twice — both times in the insurance conversation, never as a thing that takes crew time, needs disassembly, or needs specific handling.

Save Your Ass entirely absent — 0/10, on the highest-value Save-Your-Ass call in the batch. The customer said 'we haven't really packed' and estimated her own box count at 'fifteen to sixty, I have no idea,' she is on a second floor with an elevator she described as broken more often than not, and she is moving to a house with a driveway. Every one of those facts is a reason for the prep speech and none of it was given. The consolidation examples and 'take a carload' would have cut real hours off a job she is paying for by the hour, and they would have given her something to do with the week of anxiety she is clearly carrying.

No BOLDED-details framing and no 'reply with any corrections' ask on the confirmation email, so the email_handoff differentiator does not count. He committed to sending it fast — 'you can be expecting it within like a minute of us hopping off the phone' — but never told her to read it back and flag anything wrong. On a booking assembled from a verbally recited inventory with a box count between fifteen and sixty, asking her to verify in writing is not a formality.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' before the close, and no hours given — 'you can just shoot us an email or give us a call' with no window attached.
Customer's name used once, and awkwardly, in the sign-off: 'you have a good rest of your week. Weekend hunter. I guess.' He had her full name spelled out in the first minute.
Ecobox or Sparefoot never offered, on a customer who told him she has fifty to sixty boxes to pack and has not started.

A misquoted number cost real credibility mid-call. He said '$1,886 for the full thing,' the customer went quiet and then said 'Wait, I'm sorry,' and it took three turns to unwind ('1186 I said eight did I say 1886. I'm so sorry'). She had done her own arithmetic, gotten a different answer, and started doubting herself — 'I don't know what I was doing, honestly' — over his error.
top_strength: Landon converted the hardest customer in the batch, and the two moments that did it are both worth clipping. The first is the On-Time Guarantee, which he delivered not as a script line but as the direct answer to her actual fear. She said 'I'm not trying to be rude. I had really bad experience with our last movers... are they actually going to be there between 8:30 or nine or am I gonna be waiting until like ten?' and he answered with the mechanism: 'we have an on time guarantee... if we don't make it within the agreed upon arrival time. So, 8:30 to nine, we start discounting the move from the start.' When she pushed on whether Einstein would weasel out of it — 'you're not gonna be like, oh, well there is more traffic' — he closed it flat: 'No, no, no, it's in place, the agreed start time is 8:30 to nine. So if we make it outside of that, we're not obligated but we uphold that is the best way to put it.' Then he went further than he had to and volunteered the crew-quality answer she had not asked for: 'all of our guys, they're employed by us so we don't have any contracted movers so they're all vetted and have thorough background checks and we do a really long interview process. So we make sure we're really picky.' That is a bad-prior-experience objection fully closed. The second is his insurance explanation, which is the best in the batch by some distance and the only one that used the industry baseline correctly: 'the state requires us to have just like general liability insurance, that's like 60 cents per pound per item, that doesn't account for stuff like a Peloton, some of the nicer stuff you have. So we just kind of have that little bit of protection built in.' He named the $2,000 No Worries coverage, framed it against 60 cents a pound, and anchored it to her actual Peloton rather than a hypothetical — and when she asked 'Is that an additional cost?' he answered 'No, no, not at all. It's just built into the rate.' His rate work was equally clean: he broke $202 into '$101 an hour for each individual mover,' proactively steered her to the cheapest day before she asked for a discount ('for Friday, Saturday our rates are more expensive. Sunday is actually the best value day we have. So I was gonna recommend shoot for Sunday'), disclosed the $75 trip fee unprompted the moment he had the McKinney address, and gave her the no-deposit and no-cancellation-fee terms before she asked. He also owned his own mistakes instantly and twice — 'That's on me. I just gave you the wrong number,' and, on the differentiators he had skipped, 'I'm supposed to kind of go over that stuff as well. I kinda drop the ball on it.' A rep who audits himself out loud mid-call is a rep who is coachable.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is the one that could cost this specific job: Landon booked a move without ever explaining the clock. No start trigger, no 2.5-hour minimum, no fifteen-minute proration, no sense-check — 0 out of 4. Hunter is now on the schedule for Sunday at 8:30 believing the number is $1,287, and she does not know when billing starts, when it stops, what happens if it runs long, or how overage is measured. This is the customer who opened by telling him she had a bad experience with her last movers. If Sunday runs to seven hours because the elevator is down and the box count lands at sixty, the conversation on her driveway is going to be about a number she was never taught to read. The fix is ninety seconds before the booking confirm: 'Quick on how the clock works so there are no surprises — the guys open the contract when they get there at 8:30, that's when time starts. There's a two-and-a-half hour minimum, and after that we bill in fifteen-minute increments, so you only pay for what you actually use. It stops when the last item is off the truck. Does that make sense?' He has the trust to deliver that easily; he just never did. Second priority: Save Your Ass, absent on the call that needed it most. She has fifty to sixty boxes she has not packed, a second-floor apartment with an unreliable elevator, and an hourly crew. The prep speech is not a script obligation here, it is the answer to her real problem: 'One thing that'll save you actual money on Sunday — anything small and awkward, take a carload over yourself this week. The loose stuff in drawers, closet odds and ends, the art off the walls. And get everything boxed and stacked by the door before 8:30 so the guys are carrying, not sorting. If that elevator's down, every box you've already moved is one fewer trip down the stairwell on your clock. Does that make sense?' That answer also directly de-risks the estimate. Estimate-accuracy flag: he stated the typical two-bedroom range as four to six hours, said 'I don't think you're at the highest range of that for six hours,' estimated five to five and a half, and then set the record at six. Six is defensible on its face, but look at what is stacked against it — a box count she put at 'fifteen to sixty' and that he mentally rounded to fifty, a king bed, a Peloton, a second floor, an elevator she says is frequently broken, a thirty-minute drive, and no packing done a week out. That is the underestimating-side risk, and it is worth noting that he said 'better to overestimate than underestimate' out loud and then did not act on it. The coaching is not 'pad it' — it is 'resolve the variable.' The box count was never nailed down and it swings this job by two hours. 'Let's do this: text me a photo of the closets and the storage bin this week and I'll adjust the estimate before Sunday' converts a sixty-box guess into a real number. This is a booked job with a soft input, which makes it a good candidate for the estimate-versus-actual pull. Third: use her name. Once, in the sign-off, with an 'I guess' attached — on a fifteen-minute call where he had her first and last name spelled out in minute one and built genuine rapport for the other fourteen. Fourth, smaller but avoidable: slow down on the numbers. The $1,886 slip sent the customer into three turns of self-doubt about her own math. Say the total once, slowly, and let it land.
phone_presence_notes: The clearest rapport-to-conversion line in the batch — he defused her anxiety repeatedly and without condescension ('you're good, you're good. No, you're fine, like I said the same thing you said'), congratulated her on her marriage when she mentioned it in passing, owned both of his own mistakes out loud ('That's on me,' 'I kinda drop the ball on it'), and turned a customer who opened with 'I had really bad experience with our last movers' into a booking and four separate thank-yous; the one blemish on an otherwise 5 is that he used her name exactly once, in the sign-off.
